stories.headline: AI stocks drag markets down worldwide while oil jumps to $113, its highest since May, on fears of a new US-Israel strike on Iran
stories.dek: The Nasdaq fell 2.6% and the S&P 500 had its worst day since July. Nvidia, Meta and chip-tool maker Lam Research all slid even after decent results.
stories.caveman: On Thursday Oct. 22, tech stocks fell hard around the world. In the US, the Nasdaq (full of tech companies) dropped 2.6% and the S&P 500 fell 1.2%. Oddly, most US stocks actually rose; the few giant AI companies are so big that they pulled the whole index down. Nvidia fell 4.4%. Meta lost 7% even though sales beat forecasts. Lam Research, which makes chip-making machines, fell almost 12% after good results. CoreWeave, which borrowed heavily to buy AI chips and rent them out, fell 10%. Why? Investors worry that building AI data centres has become very expensive to borrow for, and that AI share prices rose too far, too fast. The selling started in Asia: South Korea's Kospi fell 3.5% and Japan's Nikkei 2.7%. At the same time, oil got pricier. Brent crude, the world benchmark, jumped 4% to $113.17 a barrel. The New York Times reported that the US and Israel have plans for 'short but intensive' new strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections. President Trump said 'something one way or the other' will happen 'fairly soon'. The US also told non-emergency staff to leave Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks there.
stories.why_it_matters: Many pensions and savings funds hold big AI companies, so their swings hit ordinary savers. Higher oil prices feed into petrol, shipping and food costs everywhere, including Taiwan, whose stock market also fell sharply the same day.
stories.camps: Worried investors: they say AI firms are spending and borrowing too much and prices have run ahead of profits. Calmer view: AI companies keep reporting growth, and one fund manager told CNBC that '$100 oil today is very different' from decades ago, since petrol takes a smaller share of US household income than it used to. Unknown: whether and when new strikes on Iran happen, which will move oil most.

stories.image_credit: Photo: Richard Drew/AP via The Guardian

stories.headline: Barclays will cut about 5,000 jobs, around 5% of its staff, as its bosses praise AI for making workers more productive
stories.dek: The British bank's profits rose. About 60% of the cuts hit support jobs, including fewer software developers. A big union says AI is being used as an excuse.
stories.caveman: Barclays is one of Britain's biggest banks, with about 93,000 staff around the world. On Oct. 22 it said it will cut about 5,000 full-time jobs as part of a plan to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. It has already cut 1,000 jobs since January. The finance chief, Anna Cross, said about 60% of the cuts are in 'support functions', including 'fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive'. Asked how many cuts were directly caused by AI, CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan said most savings so far came from wider tech investment and simpler processes, calling AI the 'icing on the cake', with possibly a bigger role later. All this came as Barclays reported strong results, including a 6% rise in interest income from UK retail banking.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a clear real-world example of a big employer linking job cuts to AI, and coding jobs are not safe. It feeds a wider question: when AI makes companies more profitable, who gets the benefit, shareholders or workers?
stories.camps: Bank's view: leaders say AI and modern technology make the bank more efficient and competitive. Union view: Unite's Sharon Graham said Barclays is 'using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce' and should retrain staff instead. Bigger picture: the cuts come while profits are up, which makes the case harder for the bank to argue it had no choice.

stories.image_credit: Photo: John Keeble/Getty Images via The Guardian

stories.headline: Japan's core inflation hits 2.1%, the highest this year, as costly energy and a weak yen push up prices
stories.dek: It jumped from 1.7% in August. The Bank of Japan, which already raised rates to a 30-year high of 1.25% in September, may raise them again.
stories.caveman: 'Inflation' is how fast prices rise. For decades Japan had the opposite problem: prices barely moved or even fell. Now that is changing. In September, Japan's 'core' inflation, which leaves out fresh food because its price jumps around, was 2.1%, up from 1.7% the month before. The 'core-core' number, which also leaves out energy and is the central bank's favourite, was 2.4%. Two reasons: energy is pricier, and Japan is buying more oil from the US instead of the Middle East, which costs more; and the yen is weak, so everything imported costs more. Japan's finance minister, Satsuki Katayama, told parliament that Japan is 'on the cusp' of steady inflation driven by rising wages. The Bank of Japan raised its interest rate in September to 1.25%, its highest in three decades, and may raise it again this year.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan is the world's fourth-biggest economy and a key trading partner for Taiwan. If its interest rates keep rising, money can flow back to Japan from around the world, which can shake markets and currencies, including the Taiwan dollar.
stories.camps: Upbeat view: the government says wages are finally rising, so mild inflation can be healthy after decades of stuck prices. Worried view: if prices rise mainly because of expensive imports and a weak yen, households feel poorer, not richer. Policy debate: raising rates fights inflation but makes loans costlier for families and companies.
stories.image_alt: Shoppers at a market in Japan

stories.headline: L'Oréal says weight-loss drugs like Ozempic are changing what people buy for their skin, and it is selling products for the 'loose skin' side effect
stories.dek: The world's biggest beauty company still grew sales 7.7% last quarter. Its brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's now market products to people on GLP-1 drugs.
stories.caveman: GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were made for diabetes, but they also cut appetite, so millions now use them to lose weight. Losing weight fast can leave some people with looser, saggier skin, including on the face. On Oct. 22 L'Oréal, which owns Maybelline, La Roche-Posay and Kiehl's, said these drugs are 'a very important phenomenon' and are 'having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular'. Its boss, Nicolas Hieronimus, said some of its brands now sell products designed to 'complement GLP-1 and its side effects on skin sagging'. L'Oréal also owns 20% of Galderma, which makes injectable fillers. Both firms are testing products on GLP-1 users. Sales still rose 7.7% in July to September, better than expected.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how one medical trend can ripple across many industries, from food and clothes to beauty. It also shows how companies turn a new body worry into a new product to sell.
stories.camps: Business view: L'Oréal sees a new market and says beauty spending is holding up well. Critical view: some health and body-image advocates worry about marketing that tells people to fix every change in their body, and about the push toward cosmetic injections. Fact to keep in mind: loose skin comes from rapid weight loss itself, not directly from the drugs.
stories.image_alt: Image accompanying the BBC report on L'Oréal and weight-loss drugs

stories.headline: 'PHP2Shell': huge flaws in the language behind most websites trigger NSA and FBI warnings, and AI is speeding up both the hunt and the attacks
stories.dek: AI tools from OpenAI and Google's Wiz helped find the bugs, but details leaked before the fix was ready. Amazon says attackers were already trying them before disclosure.
stories.caveman: PHP is a programming language from the 1990s that runs behind the scenes on just under 70% of websites whose server code is known. In August, researchers at an AI security firm called Calif and at Google's Wiz used AI models, including OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Google's Gemini, to find two serious bugs in every PHP setup that serves web pages. Together they're called 'PHP2Shell'. They let a stranger with no password run their own code on a website's server, and possibly steal data. The fix was due Thursday, but news leaked online and Calif accidentally posted a demo video, so the PHP Foundation rushed out patches a day early on Wednesday Oct. 21. The US National Security Agency told organisations to patch right away or take servers offline. Some European government sites went dark. The FBI and agencies in the UK, Canada, Australia, Singapore and the EU also issued alerts. Amazon says it saw attempts to exploit the bugs even before they were public.
stories.why_it_matters: Your bank, shop and government websites may run PHP. Experts say AI has changed the speed of cyber threats: holes that once took hackers weeks to find can now be exploited in hours, so slow patching is far riskier.
stories.camps: Alarmed view: a researcher told CNBC this level of urgency is 'very new', because 'everyone has AI-augmented capabilities', attackers and defenders alike. Cautious view: the PHP Foundation's director said there was no evidence yet of working attacks, 'only incomplete, misguided, and non-working generated ones'. Tech companies' view: OpenAI and Google highlight that their AI helped find and fix the bugs, which also serves their own marketing.
stories.image_alt: Software developers working at computers

stories.headline: OpenAI nears a deal to raise up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, led by investors from the UAE
stories.dek: The money would be a bridge before a possible stock-market listing. OpenAI is also negotiating to get more computing power from the UAE.
stories.caveman: OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, is close to raising up to $30 billion, CNBC reported on Oct. 22, citing people who know the deal. That would value the company at $1.25 trillion, making it worth more than almost any company on Earth. Investors from the United Arab Emirates, a rich Gulf state, are leading the round with the US fund Coatue. OpenAI wants signatures by the end of next week, but the final size isn't fixed. It is also negotiating a deal for more computing capacity in the UAE. OpenAI told investors in February it aims to spend about $600 billion on computing by 2030. It secretly filed papers for a stock-market listing (an IPO) in June. Its finance chief said it 'will be a public company in 2027', though CEO Sam Altman said in September that now would be 'an ill-advised moment to go public'.
stories.why_it_matters: AI needs enormous amounts of money and electricity. Whoever pays for it gains influence over a technology that many people use daily. Gulf states are using oil wealth to buy a big role in AI.
stories.camps: Supporters: investors see OpenAI as a leader in a technology that could reshape the economy, worth paying a huge price for. Skeptics: the same day, AI stocks were sliding on fears of a bubble; a $1.25 trillion price for a company that spends far more than it earns looks risky to some. Concerns about influence: critics question giving autocratic Gulf governments a big stake and data-centre role in key AI systems.
stories.image_alt: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on stage in front of the OpenAI logo

stories.headline: Meta creates a new kind of share so Mark Zuckerberg can pay a possible California billionaire tax without leaving the state; its stock sinks 7%
stories.dek: Californians vote early next month on Prop 40, a one-time 5% tax on about 250 billionaires. Meta's AI spending also pushed its cash flow below zero.
stories.caveman: California will vote on Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of the roughly 250 billionaires who live there. Mark Zuckerberg, Meta's boss, is worth about $239bn, so he could owe billions. He told Meta he was thinking of moving. On Oct. 21 Meta announced a deal: it will split every share into two and create new 'class C' shares that have no voting power. Zuckerberg can sell those to pay the tax without losing control of the company. In return he promises to stay living in California, or wherever Meta is based, for eight years. The same night Meta reported sales up 26% to $64.6bn, beating forecasts, but profit fell 37%, partly because of a $9.9bn charge linked to a lawsuit over child safety and social media addiction. Meta also spent so much on AI that its 'free cash flow' was minus $2.1bn for the quarter, and it raised its yearly spending plan to $135bn–$145bn. Shares fell nearly 7% on Oct. 22.
stories.why_it_matters: This mixes three big debates: how much the very rich should pay in tax, how much control company founders keep, and whether giant AI spending will pay off.
stories.camps: For the tax: US congressman Ro Khanna says Prop 40 is a choice between workers and 'oligarchs', and that billionaires should pay their fair share. Against: tech billionaires such as Sergey Brin and Peter Thiel are spending heavily to defeat it, warning the rich will leave the state; polls show it short of majority support. On Meta's deal: critics say the company is using shareholders' structure to shield its boss's personal tax bill; Meta says it keeps its 'founder-led structure' stable.
stories.image_alt: Mark Zuckerberg with his wife Priscilla Chan
stories.image_credit: Photo: Mario Anzuoni/Reuters via The Guardian

stories.headline: Etsy bans AI-made recipes, knitting and sewing patterns, and makes sellers show a real photo of the finished item
stories.dek: The craft marketplace says many shoppers can't tell what's made with AI, and it's now a top-three reason they don't shop more. AI art is still allowed if disclosed.
stories.caveman: Etsy is a US website where people sell handmade and vintage things, plus digital downloads like crochet patterns. Lately it has filled up with AI 'slop': patterns and recipes written by AI that may not even work. On Oct. 22 Etsy said it will ban AI-made 'functional guides', meaning patterns, cooking recipes and instructions, where a buyer puts in effort to make something. Sellers must show a photo of a real item made with the instructions, not an AI-faked result, and at least one unedited photo of what they sell. Fully bot-made listings with no human involved are banned. AI-generated art can stay, as long as sellers play a clear role and disclose it. Etsy said buyers' confusion about AI is a 'top-three barrier' to shopping, and real makers worried about being drowned out.
stories.why_it_matters: It's one of the first big online shops to draw a firm line on AI content. Other platforms face the same flood of cheap AI products and fake photos.
stories.camps: Makers and buyers: many welcome it, saying AI copies flooded the site and undercut real crafters. Sellers who use AI: some may lose income or find the rules hard to follow. Mixed signals: critics note Etsy still uses AI itself, to profile shoppers and power a ChatGPT shopping app with OpenAI.

stories.headline: Russia fires 21 missiles at Kyiv just hours after Putin agreed to restart peace talks; Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink
stories.dek: At least two people were killed and 22 wounded, including four children. Zelenskyy says Russia used cluster warheads and chose civilian areas on purpose.
stories.caveman: On Wednesday Oct. 21 US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg and praised him as 'a humanitarian'. The Kremlin said Putin agreed 'in principle' to restart three-way talks with the US and Ukraine after Nov. 10, a week after the US midterm elections. Overnight, Russia hit Kyiv with three waves of ballistic missiles, 21 in all, according to Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. At least two people died and 22 were hurt. Targets included a bridge over the Dnipro River, homes, energy sites, an ambulance station and a clinic. Zelenskyy said three missiles carried cluster warheads, and one damaged historic buildings including a monastery. Separately, Ukraine's military satellite internet, run by Elon Musk's Starlink, had been slowed, hurting its drones and missile warnings. Trump said on Oct. 22 that Musk 'put it back', though Zelenskyy said speed wasn't fully restored. Musk denies he caused the slowdown.
stories.why_it_matters: Talks about peace mean little if bombing continues. And the Starlink episode shows how much a war can depend on one private billionaire's company.
stories.camps: Ukraine's view: Zelenskyy says the attack proves Russia isn't serious about peace and asks for more Patriot air defences and sanctions; its foreign minister said 'flattery' won't stop Russia. UK view: Downing Street rejected Witkoff's description of Putin. Trump side: the White House pushes for a deal and has waived some Russia sanctions ahead of the midterms; it denies ordering any Starlink slowdown.
stories.image_alt: A woman looks at her damaged apartment after a Russian missile attack in Kyiv
stories.image_credit: Photo: Efrem Lukatsky/AP via The Guardian

stories.headline: Iran threatens to hit oil sites, undersea cables and AI data centres in up to seven Gulf countries if the US and Israel attack again
stories.dek: US media report plans for new strikes after the Nov. 3 midterms. Iran-backed Houthis killed two at a Saudi airport, and the US told some staff to leave Saudi Arabia.
stories.caveman: The US and Israel fought Iran earlier, and talks to end the conflict are stuck. US media say American and Israeli planners have drawn up targets for a new joint attack after the US midterm elections on Nov. 3. On Oct. 22 Mohsen Rezaei, a top Iranian security official, said that if that happens, Iran could strike oil facilities, undersea internet cables, data centres and AI sites across as many as seven Gulf countries. An adviser to Iran's lead negotiator called a third war in two years an 'existential threat' and said Iran's strategy is 'zero red lines'. Meanwhile Yemen's Houthis, allies of Iran, said they hit King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia; Saudi officials said two people died and eight were hurt. Two more people died from a downed drone's debris near an Aramco oil site. Diplomats from Europe, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt meet in Istanbul on Friday.
stories.why_it_matters: Gulf countries supply a huge share of the world's oil and are building giant AI data centres. A wider war could push fuel prices even higher and threaten internet cables that carry global data.
stories.camps: Iran's view: officials say they will not accept attacks on Iran's economy while the Gulf facilities that support those attacks stay safe. US and Israel: officials have briefed about possible strikes on missile, oil and nuclear sites, arguing Iran must not get nuclear weapons. Regional states: many fear being caught in the middle; they are meeting to try to agree a common approach. Note: Trump has backed away from new strikes seven times in four months.

stories.image_credit: Photo: Mohammed Salem/Reuters via The Guardian

stories.headline: Serbia votes Sunday in a snap election that could end Vučić's 12-year grip, with a leaderless student movement as his main challenger
stories.dek: Protests began after a train-station roof collapse killed 16 people in 2024. Observers worry about media bias, voter pressure and errors in the voter list.
stories.caveman: On Nov. 1, 2024, a concrete canopy at the newly renovated train station in Novi Sad, Serbia's second city, fell and killed 16 people. Many Serbians blamed corruption and sloppy work, and the project was closely tied to President Aleksandar Vučić. Students began weekly protests demanding justice. They grew into a national movement joined by farmers, actors and judges; the prime minister resigned. Now there's a snap parliamentary election on Sunday Oct. 25. Vučić stepped down as president to lead his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) list and try to become prime minister. His main rival is the 'Student List', a group with no single leader that picks respected local doctors, teachers and professionals as candidates. Its lead candidate, cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, says 'the energy is unstoppable'. The old opposition parties have shrunk to 10–15% support. Thursday Oct. 22 was the last day of campaigning.
stories.why_it_matters: Serbia wants to join the EU but also stays close to Russia and China. A disputed result could bring mass protests and instability in the Balkans.
stories.camps: Student List and supporters: they say the vote is a referendum on corruption and want accountable institutions. Vučić's camp: his party relies on nationalist voters, state resources and friendly media, and calls the protesters a threat to stability. Watchdogs: the Guardian notes media bias, voter intimidation and voter-list problems mean any result could be contested. Context: Vučić's government gave a hero's funeral last month to convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić, angering many abroad.
stories.image_alt: Young Serbians, the driving force behind the student movement

stories.headline: Days before Brazil's runoff, Lula asks the top election court to disqualify Flávio Bolsonaro over claims Meta limited Lula's posts
stories.dek: UN experts say they're worried about reports that one campaign was curbed on Facebook and Instagram. Meta denies favouring either side; Bolsonaro filed his own petition.
stories.caveman: Brazil picks its president in a final round (a runoff) on Sunday Oct. 25: left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. On Oct. 21 Lula's campaign asked Brazil's top electoral court to disqualify Bolsonaro, accusing Meta (owner of WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook) of limiting Lula's content to help his rival. The same day, a UN report led by the special rapporteur on freedom of expression said 'information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed'. It mentioned temporary shutdowns of one campaign account and limits on its Instagram posts. Users also said Meta's AI tools wouldn't make images of Lula. Bolsonaro hit back with a petition to disqualify Lula over mass sharing of government posts on WhatsApp. Meta denies unequal treatment and says it will follow a court order to treat both equally.
stories.why_it_matters: Social media now shapes elections everywhere. If a platform tilts what voters see, even by accident, it can affect who wins, which is a worry for Taiwan's elections too.
stories.camps: Lula's side: says Meta's actions are illegal interference that helped Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro's side: says Lula is abusing government channels and that the complaint is a desperate move before the vote. Meta: denies taking sides. Neutral note: disqualifying a finalist days before a vote would be extreme; courts may order fixes instead.
stories.image_alt: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, who meet in Sunday's runoff

stories.headline: HOT: Jeff Kinney takes 'Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight' on the road with pyrotechnics, a boxing ring and a Wicked Witch
stories.dek: The newest book in the bestselling kids' series tackles survival in middle school. Kinney gave $1,000 in books to an Ohio school library on tour.
stories.caveman: 'Diary of a Wimpy Kid' is a hugely popular US children's book series about a middle-schooler named Greg Heffley, told in diary entries with cartoon drawings. Author Jeff Kinney's new book, 'Fight or Flight' (Amulet Books), puts Greg in a chicken suit with boxing gloves on the cover. Kinney said he wanted to write about 'survival in the halls of middle school' while keeping the jokes. On Oct. 18 he and his team set off on a tour in a custom 'Wimpy Wagon' van. The events are now full stage shows: fireworks-style effects, a stage set up like a boxing ring, and characters such as the Wicked Witch of the West and a baby Yeti. At a school in Columbus, Ohio, on Oct. 21, he surprised students with $1,000 of new books for their library. The tour heads to Canada, Ireland and the UK in November. Kinney also runs a bookshop, An Unlikely Story, in his Massachusetts town.
stories.why_it_matters: Books that turn kids into eager readers matter, especially as reading for fun declines. Kinney's live shows turn a book release into an event families want to attend.
stories.camps: Fans and booksellers: the shows bring crowds to indie bookstores and get kids excited about reading. Skeptics: some critics say mega-series take up shelf space and attention that could go to newer or more diverse authors. Context: see the 'NOT' story; many less famous authors are losing school visits.
stories.image_alt: The decorated 'Fight or Flight' tour van for Jeff Kinney's Wimpy Kid book tour

terms.explain: Books for readers about 8 to 12 years old.
A trip where an author visits stores and schools to promote a new book.
An independently owned bookshop, not part of a big chain.
Fireworks-style effects used in shows.

stories.headline: NOT: US children's authors are getting far fewer school visits as school districts slash budgets, and poorer schools lose out most
stories.dek: Over half of the 50 biggest US school districts cut budgets. For some picture-book authors, school visits are half their income.
stories.caveman: Many children's authors earn a big part of their living by visiting schools to talk about books and writing. This school year those bookings are falling. Education site Chalkbeat found well over half of America's 50 largest school districts recently cut budgets, because of fewer students (falling birth rates, more homeschooling and private schools). Phil Bildner, who runs a booking agency for over 80 authors, told PW most of them have 'far fewer' public-school visits booked. Rules have also piled up: many schools now require authors to carry business insurance. Author Maggie Tokuda-Hall says visits are half her income. Visits are often paid with federal 'Title I' money for high-poverty schools, now stretched thin. A literacy professor, Emily Pendergrass, says visits get cut because they're seen as 'enrichment rather than essential instruction'.
stories.why_it_matters: Meeting a real author can spark a lifelong love of reading. If only rich schools can pay, kids in poorer areas lose that chance, and fewer authors can afford to write full time.
stories.camps: Equity concern: Pendergrass says 'the larger concern is equity' if visits depend on parent fundraising. Authors: Tokuda-Hall says the gap between public and private schools is widening, and famous authors grab the remaining slots. School side: districts facing shortfalls say they must protect core teaching and staff first. Policy link: voucher laws moving students to private schools shrink public budgets further.
stories.image_alt: Two children's book authors quoted in the story about school visits

terms.explain: The local authority that runs public schools in an area of the US.
US federal money for schools with many low-income students.
Extra activities beyond core lessons, like trips or author visits.
Public money given to families to spend on private school fees.
Fairness, making sure everyone gets what they need to have the same chances.

stories.headline: FIGHT: Court rules a Florida school board can't hide behind 'legislative privilege' and must explain why it pulled library books
stories.dek: PEN America, Penguin Random House and authors sued Escambia County. A federal appeals panel, including a Trump-appointed judge, ruled 2–1.
stories.caveman: In 2023 a teacher in Escambia County, Florida, challenged nine books, saying they had 'pornography', 'race-baiting' and an 'LGBTQ agenda using penguins' (that last one is a picture book about two male penguins raising a chick). The school board removed or restricted hundreds of books, sometimes against its own review committee's advice. Free-speech group PEN America, publisher Penguin Random House, authors and a parent sued, saying the board targeted books by or about people of color and LGBTQ people, breaking the US Constitution. When they tried to question board members, the board claimed 'legislative privilege', a shield that protects lawmakers from testifying about their law-making. On Oct. 19 a panel of the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 2–1 that choosing library books is an administrative act, not law-making, so the shield doesn't apply. Judge Andrew Brasher, a Trump appointee, wrote the opinion.
stories.why_it_matters: Across the US, book removals have surged. This ruling means officials can be made to explain their reasons under oath, which could shape many similar cases.
stories.camps: PEN America: says 'the freedom to read demands accountability' and it's eager to question board members. School board side: argues elected boards should decide what is age-appropriate for local children and has appealed twice. Wider split: supporters of removals say parents' rights are at stake; opponents say a few complaints shouldn't decide what all students can read, especially since parents can already opt their own children out.
stories.image_alt: Books on a school library shelf

terms.explain: A legal shield that stops lawmakers being forced to testify about making laws.
A higher court that reviews decisions made by lower courts.
The part of the US Constitution protecting free speech, press and religion.
A US writers' group that defends free expression.
Questioning someone under oath outside the courtroom, before a trial.

stories.headline: SPLIT: America's public libraries team up with Microsoft to teach staff and patrons about AI, while the company warns of 'cognitive offloading'
stories.dek: The Public Library Association's free webinars and practice sessions aim to answer questions about using AI responsibly. Some see a tech giant shaping how libraries think about its products.
stories.caveman: Libraries are trusted places where people go to learn new skills, and lots of people now come with questions about AI. The Public Library Association (PLA), part of the American Library Association, announced 'Building AI Skills and Agency Through Libraries', a free program with four webinars and community practice sessions for library workers and the public. It's built with Microsoft Elevate, a Microsoft unit focused on AI skills for schools, libraries, unions and nonprofits. Its president, Justin Spelhaug, said libraries can help people use AI 'in a way that's safe'. He also warned about 'cognitive offloading', when people let AI do their thinking, which can block real learning, especially for young people. PLA members had asked for staff training, community classes and examples of AI policies.
stories.why_it_matters: Like it or not, AI is in daily life. Libraries could help people use it wisely, but who designs the lessons shapes what people learn.
stories.camps: Supporters: PLA's president Jamar Rahming says it will help library workers support people asking 'how AI can be used responsibly and thoughtfully'. Skeptics: some librarians and critics worry about a company that sells AI teaching the public about AI, and about privacy and dependence on one vendor. Middle ground: Microsoft says it will adapt its safety, privacy and transparency standards for libraries with PLA and ALA input.
stories.image_alt: Public Library Association and Microsoft AI skills program graphic

terms.explain: Public Library Association, the US group for public libraries, part of the American Library Association.
A seminar or class held online.
Letting a tool do your thinking or remembering for you.
Knowing what AI is, how it works, and how to use it wisely and safely.
A person who uses a library.

stories.headline: BBC investigation: Sudan's RSF deliberately attacked hospitals in el-Fasher at least 43 times; UN rights chief says it may amount to war crimes
stories.dek: Over two and a half years, 55 health workers were killed and 120 injured in the city. The RSF calls the findings propaganda.
stories.caveman: Sudan has been in civil war since April 2023 between the army and a paramilitary group called the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). El-Fasher, a big city in the western Darfur region, was besieged and fell to the RSF about a year ago, one of the war's most brutal chapters. Using sources who were on the ground, the BBC found at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and health sites from May 2024 to October 2025, some hit more than once. Between April 2023 and October 2025, 55 medical workers were killed, 120 injured and 10 'disappeared' or kidnapped. A surgeon who worked there told the BBC the attacks were 'deliberate' and 'planned' to empty the city. UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings 'deeply disturbing'. Attacking hospitals during war is illegal under international law. The army has also been accused: in March 2026 a drone strike, believed to be by the army, hit a hospital in RSF-held East Darfur.
stories.why_it_matters: Sudan has one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with millions forced from their homes, but gets little attention. Evidence like this can matter for future justice.
stories.camps: Investigators and the UN: say this may amount to war crimes and the attackers must be held to account. RSF: rejects the BBC's findings as a smear campaign by the army and its allies. Fairness note: both sides have been accused of attacking health facilities.
stories.image_alt: Image from the BBC investigation into attacks on hospitals in el-Fasher

terms.explain: Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group fighting Sudan's army.
An armed group organised like an army but not the official military.
Surrounding a place to cut off supplies and force it to give up.
A serious breach of the laws of war, like deliberately attacking civilians or hospitals.
A large region in western Sudan.

stories.headline: Born premature as fighting surged, seven-week-old twins in Yemen battle severe malnutrition after their family fled on foot for three days
stories.dek: As war between the Houthis and government forces flares again, baby-milk prices have soared and hospitals in Aden are filling with starving children.
stories.caveman: Yemen's civil war pits the Iran-backed Houthi rebels against government forces. When fighting reached their mountain village in south-west Yemen, a family of seven fled bombs, missiles and drones, carrying newborn twins Raghad and Raad, born early and protected only by blankets. They walked for three days before a stranger drove them to the port city of Aden. By the time they reached al-Sadaqah hospital, the babies were 'just skin and bone', a doctor said. Their father, a shepherd, said he could feed them only twice a day, sometimes only water, because the war pushed up the price of baby milk. Doctors diagnosed severe acute malnutrition, which the BBC notes can be as deadly as a bullet. Raad was barely bigger than a nurse's hands.
stories.why_it_matters: Wars kill not only with weapons but with hunger. Children under five are the most at risk, and Yemen's crisis is getting worse as Gulf tensions rise.
stories.camps: Aid groups: say more funding and safe access for food and medicine are urgently needed. Warring sides: each blames the other for the fighting and blockades that push up prices. Bigger picture: renewed clashes linked to the wider Iran conflict make relief harder to deliver.
stories.image_alt: The twins' family, who walked for three days before getting a lift to Aden

terms.explain: When the body doesn't get enough of the food it needs.
Born too early, before the baby is fully developed.
An Iran-backed rebel group that controls much of northern Yemen.
Forced to leave home because of war or disaster.

stories.headline: Nearly 1 in 10 adults in England and Wales suffered domestic abuse in the past year, up from 7.8%, driven by partner abuse, official survey finds
stories.dek: About 4.7 million people were affected. Women were hit most, but 2.1 million men too. Charities say the government is off track on its promise to halve violence against women and girls.
stories.caveman: Domestic abuse means hurting or controlling someone at home or in a relationship: hitting, threats, controlling money, or constant put-downs. Britain's Office for National Statistics interviews over 30,000 adults a year for its Crime Survey for England and Wales. Its latest numbers, for the year to March 2026, show 9.6% of people 16 and over (about 4.7 million) experienced domestic abuse, up from 7.8% (3.8 million) the year before. The rise came mostly from abuse by partners; family abuse barely changed. Women were more affected: 12.8%, or about 3.2 million, compared with 8.9% of men, about 2.1 million. New questions also found 2.1% suffered sexual victimisation and 3.9% were stalked. In total, almost 11% of adults suffered at least one of these. The ONS says small survey changes may affect the numbers, but the rise 'includes real change'.
stories.why_it_matters: The UK government promised to halve violence against women and girls by 2034, and this survey is the main way it will be measured. It also shows that abuse is common, and men can be victims too.
stories.camps: Charities: Refuge says the data 'tells a troubling story' and the government is not on track. Statisticians: the ONS urges caution because of survey changes and says more years of data are needed. Government: says the figures will guide its strategy. Helpful context: more people recognising abuse can also raise reported numbers.
stories.image_alt: An illustrative image accompanying a report on domestic abuse figures
stories.image_credit: Photo: Tinnakorn Jorruang/Shutterstock via The Guardian

terms.explain: Violence or control by a partner or family member.
Office for National Statistics, the UK's official number-crunching agency.
Repeatedly following, watching or contacting someone in a way that scares them.
How common something is in a group of people.
A UK charity that helps women and children escaping domestic abuse.

stories.headline: A magnitude-7 earthquake hits Tibet at night, killing at least 16 people and collapsing 339 homes
stories.dek: Rockfalls closed roads to the high-altitude area, slowing rescuers. The region was also hit by deadly glacier floods less than two months ago.
stories.caveman: On Thursday night Oct. 22, a strong earthquake of magnitude 7 struck Baqên County in the Nagqu region of Tibet, about 400km north-east of the capital, Lhasa, Chinese state media reported. At least 16 people died and 32 were injured. Power was cut and 339 homes collapsed. Falling rocks blocked roads, making it harder for rescue teams to reach the mountain villages. Shaking was felt in other Tibetan cities. Videos online showed villagers running into dark streets as buildings shook, though these were not independently verified. The area sits where the Indian and Eurasian plates push together, so big quakes are common. Less than two months ago, a glacier collapse caused floods and landslides in Tibet and Nepal that killed at least 1,400 people.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan also sits on a busy earthquake zone. Each disaster is a reminder of why building rules, early warnings and fast rescue matter.
stories.camps: Officials: China has declared an emergency and sent rescue teams. Rights groups and journalists: information from Tibet is tightly controlled, so independent checks of casualty numbers are hard. Science view: quakes of this size are expected in the region; the toll depends heavily on how well buildings are made.
stories.image_alt: Firefighters help residents injured by the quake in Baqên, Tibet

terms.explain: A number for an earthquake's strength; each step up is about 32 times more energy.
Giant slabs of Earth's crust that slowly move and cause quakes where they meet.
News outlets controlled by the government.
A huge, slow-moving body of ice.
